title: Polenta Morbida
subtitle: Soft, creamy northern Italian polenta
excerpt: Polenta morbida is soft, creamy northern Italian polenta made with coarse polenta flour, water, butter, and parmesan. It takes 40 to 45 minutes of stirring and produces something rich and flavoured enough to eat as a main dish with nothing more than a little extra parmesan on top.
sourceNotes: Polenta is the staple grain dish of northern Italy, particularly associated with Lombardy, Veneto, Piedmont, and Friuli-Venezia Giulia. It replaced other cereal porridges as the dominant grain food in the north from the 17th century onward, when maize was introduced to Italy from the Americas. Polenta morbida (soft polenta) is the base version; polenta is also cooled, sliced, and grilled or fried as a variation.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Soft polenta does not hold well. Cook and serve immediately. Leftover polenta can be cooled, sliced, and grilled or fried the next day.

glossaryTerms.definition: Ground dried maize (corn), available in fine and coarse grinds. Coarse polenta takes longer to cook but has a better texture. Quick-cook polenta is precooked and ready in 5 minutes, but the texture is inferior.

content.text: Soft polenta is coarse maize flour stirred slowly into simmering salted water until it thickens to a creamy, pourable consistency, then enriched with butter and parmesan. The key is patience: it needs 40 to 45 minutes of regular stirring over low heat. Quick-cook polenta is available but gives an inferior result. The finished dish is rich enough to serve as a main with just parmesan, or as a base for braised meats, mushrooms, or fried eggs.
Bring the water to a boil in a large, heavy-bottomed pot. Add the salt.
Reduce the heat to medium-low. Pour the
in a slow, steady stream, whisking continuously as you pour to prevent lumps from forming.

Switch to a wooden spoon and stir frequently over low heat for 40 to 45 minutes. The polenta will thicken, begin to bubble and spit (take care), and gradually pull away from the sides of the pot. It is ready when it tastes cooked and has no chalky raw flavour.
Remove from the heat. Add the butter and parmesan and beat vigorously with the spoon until the butter has melted and the polenta is smooth and glossy. Taste and add more salt if needed.
Serve immediately in warmed bowls with extra parmesan. Polenta thickens and sets very quickly once off the heat.

items.cause: The flour was added too quickly or not stirred fast enough as it went in.
items.fix: Use a whisk for the first 5 minutes while adding the flour. If lumps form, use a stick blender briefly to smooth them out before continuing to stir.

items.symptom: The polenta tastes grainy or raw even after 45 minutes
items.cause: The heat was too low or the polenta was not coarse grain flour.
items.fix: Increase the heat very slightly and continue cooking, tasting every 5 minutes. Some very coarse grinds need up to 60 minutes.

content.text: Polenta is the staple grain of northern Italy, particularly in Veneto, Lombardy, and Friuli. For several centuries it was the primary food for the rural poor of the north, eaten twice a day. Italians from the south sometimes refer to northerners as 'polentoni', a term that acknowledges this grain staple. Today soft polenta is served in restaurants as a base for braised meats and mushrooms, and is recognised as a distinctive part of northern Italian cooking.
